# The Weight of Inherited Terror

The archival vault beneath the palace lay silent as a tomb, its ancient stone walls lined with shelves that stretched into the oppressive darkness like the ribs of some colossal, fossilized beast. Kaedan descended the spiral staircase with careful steps, his leather boots clicking against worn obsidian, each footfall echoing through the heavy, dust-laden air. He was twenty-two years old, the newest Royal Court Wizard of Thronegate, and the blood of Blake thrummed in his veins with a potency that multiplied a thousandfold every single day he drew breath past his twentieth year. By the standards of the wider omniverse, he was already a walking cataclysm, a wizard whose suppressed mana could shatter solar systems. Yet as he reached the bottom of the stairs and gazed upon the endless rows of leather-bound journals, his stomach clenched with a cold, nauseating dread.

His father, Corin, stood waiting beside a heavy oak reading table, his weathered face illuminated by the soft, blue glow of a single hovering arcane lantern. Corin was seventy-three years old, his mutton chops now fully gray, his eyes carrying the haunted weight of a man who had witnessed things that had permanently scarred the architecture of his soul. He had served as Godric's court wizard for fifty-three years before his son came of age, and he had spent every single one of those years sleeping with a light on.

"You've read the master lore texts," Corin said, his voice a low, gravelly rasp. He gestured toward the towering shelves. "You know the history of Olympus, the Stasis Event, the Awakening. You know the official records of Thronegate's expansion. But none of that will prepare you for what is in these journals."

Kaedan swallowed hard, his throat dry. "Father, I've studied the amplification mechanics. I understand that Lord Godric's stats multiply infinitely every Planck second. I know the math—"

"The math," Corin interrupted, his voice cracking with a sudden, sharp bitterness, "is a lie. Not a deliberate lie, but a conceptual failure. Your mind, my mind, the combined intellect of the entire omniverse—none of it can actually comprehend the scale. The numbers stop meaning anything after the first sentence. What you need to understand is the feeling. The weight. The moment when you realize that everything you are, everything you will ever be, is a microscopic zero compared to a single, relaxed, unbottered cell of our sovereign's body."

Corin pulled a thick, ancient journal from the nearest shelf, its leather cover cracked and stained with what looked like ancient sweat. He placed it on the reading table with a heavy thud. "These journals were not commissioned by Lord Godric. He does not know the details of what we write, though he knows we write them. He finds it mildly amusing, I think. He believes we are overreacting. He genuinely, sincerely believes that because he always holds back to zero percent of his power, we are being dramatic."

A bitter, choked laugh escaped Corin's throat. "Zero percent. As if that phrase has any meaning when the denominator is literally infinite."

He pushed the journal toward Kaedan. "I am required to make you read these. It is a tradition enforced by every father upon his son since Blake himself. We do it to keep ourselves sane. We do it so that when you stand beside him and watch him dismantle an omniversal threat without moving a muscle, your mind does not completely shatter. It will still crack. It always cracks. But these journals are the only thing that will hold the pieces together."

Kaedan sat down at the heavy oak table, his fingers trembling slightly as he opened the first journal. The handwriting was cramped, urgent, the letters pressed so deeply into the parchment that they had scarred the fibers.

"Start with Marlon," Corin said softly. "Year 47,819. He witnessed the strength incident. He was never the same."

---

**Year 47,819 — Marlon — The Folly of Physical Force**

I have tried to write this account seventeen times. Each previous attempt ended with my hands seizing into claws, my quill snapping, my inkwell shattering against the far wall as the memory overwhelmed my motor functions. My wife believes I have developed a tremor disorder. She is wrong. I have developed a terror disorder. A dread so deeply embedded in my bone marrow that my body physically revolts against the act of remembering.

The entity called itself Gorath-That-Was, though that name is a pathetic underselling of its nature. It was not a single being but a collective consciousness of every warrior-god, every titan, every apex physical predator that had ever existed across a decillion multiverses. They had merged their physical forms into a single, unified body of pure, concentrated muscular force. The entity stood taller than googolplexian galaxy clusters, its skin forged from the compressed neutronium of dead universes, its muscles woven from the conceptual fabric of strength itself. It had shattered the dimensional barriers of an infinitude of realities simply by flexing. It had punched through the chronological walls of timelines. It had killed abstract concepts of invulnerability by headbutting them.

When it descended upon Thronegate, the sky did not tear. The sky simply ceased to exist, replaced by the infinite, crushing mass of its descending fist. The atmospheric pressure alone passively annihilated decillions of surrounding multiverses before the blow even began its trajectory. Entire civilizations, entire pantheons of gods, entire cosmic histories were erased in the microsecond before impact—not as a target, but as collateral noise.

Lord Godric was taking his morning walk through the eastern gardens. He was wearing simple sandals and a loose linen tunic. He was holding a cup of tea that Blake's wife Anna had brewed for him forty-seven thousand years ago, still steaming, preserved in a localized temporal stasis purely because he enjoyed the aroma.

He looked up at the descending fist. He did not brace. He did not shift his weight. He did not stop walking. He simply continued his casual, unhurried stride, and the fist struck the crown of his head.

The fist did not stop. It did not bounce. It did not shatter against his skull. It simply ceased to be a fist. The moment the neutronium-forged skin of the entity made contact with a single strand of Godric's salt-and-pepper hair, the entire physical structure of the attack was violently, instantly, and absolutely unmade. The kinetic energy of a googolplexian collapsing multiverses was not absorbed or deflected; it was retroactively deleted from the timeline. The entity's arm, from fingertip to shoulder joint, disintegrated into less than subatomic dust. Not atoms. Not quarks. The fundamental mathematical possibility of its physical existence was revoked.

But Godric's passive resting strength—the baseline force exerted by his completely relaxed, unbothered musculature at zero percent of his true power—did not stop at the arm. The strength stat, having multiplied recursively every infinitesimal fraction of a Planck second for over forty-seven thousand years, radiated outward from the point of contact in a silent, invisible wave of absolute physical pressure. The entire omniverse—every reality, every timeline, every dimension, every conceptual plane, every pocket of existence that had ever been or could ever be—was instantly, violently, and completely pulverized. Not destroyed. Pulverized. Crushed into a featureless, dimensionless point of absolute nothingness so thoroughly that the concept of "nothingness" itself was crushed into something even smaller.

I only survived because Lord Godric's will preserved me. I stood in the void, my lungs drawing breath that did not exist, my heart beating in a chest that should have been erased, and I watched my King continue his morning walk across the non-existent ground. He took a sip of his eternal tea. He hummed a soft, tuneless melody that I later learned was a lullaby he used to sing to his daughters in Olympus.

"Messy," he murmured, looking at the absolute nothingness surrounding us. "I did not anticipate the rebound effect. The passive resistance of my hair follicles was slightly higher than my initial estimate."

He did not wave his hand. He did not speak a word of power. He simply decided that the omniverse should exist again. In exactly zero seconds, with exactly zero effort, every single destroyed reality was perfectly restored. Every galaxy, every planet, every god, every mortal, every atom was rebuilt precisely as it had been. Their memories were intact. Their bodies were intact. But their souls—every single conscious soul in the omniverse—had experienced an inexplicable, haunting moment of absolute insignificance. A shadow had passed over their existence, and they would never, ever know why.

The entity Gorath-That-Was was not restored. Its severed arm remained severed, its body frozen in an eternal, agonizing spasm of incomplete existence, its consciousness trapped in the microsecond of its own unmasking. Lord Godric left it there, hovering in the void between restored realities, as an eternal monument to the futility of physical force.

I have written this account. My hands are bleeding. My quill is broken. My mind is fractured. But the record exists. Let it serve as warning to all who inherit my staff.

---

Kaedan closed the journal, his breath coming in short, shallow gasps. His hands were shaking so violently that the leather cover rattled against the oak table. "His hair," he whispered. "The passive resistance of his hair follicles."

"Keep reading," Corin said, his voice completely devoid of comfort. "You have barely begun."

---

**Year 312,004 — Selwyn — The Impossibility of Speed**

I am Selwyn. I am forty-one years old. I have served Lord Godric for twenty-one years, and I have not slept for the last nineteen of them. Not because I cannot sleep, but because every time I close my eyes, I see the blur. I see the absolute, incomprehensible stillness that passed for motion. I see the thing that outran causality itself being overtaken by a man who did not even shift his weight.

The opposition called themselves the Chronos Ascendancy. They were not warriors in the traditional sense. They were pure speed, entities that had shed their physical bodies eons ago to become living, sentient velocities. They existed as hyper-accelerated thought-forms, moving so fast that the Planck second—the smallest possible unit of measurable time—felt like a frozen eternity to them. They could traverse the entire omniverse, from one conceptual boundary to the other, in a time frame so small that the number of zeros after the decimal point would fill a library. They had outrun the Big Bang. They had lapped the heat death of multiverses. They had raced the concept of simultaneity and won.

They descended upon the capital world not as an invasion, but as a single, unified strike. Their plan was simple: accelerate beyond the threshold of Godric's omniscience, strike him before his passive defenses could register their existence, and erase him from the timeline before the timeline itself understood what had happened. They genuinely believed that their speed was a conceptual exploit, that the Weakness Paradox would not trigger if they moved faster than the paradox itself could process.

The Weakness Paradox triggered the instant they formed this thought, thirty thousand years before their attack. Godric's speed stat, already multiplying beyond infinitely incalculable mathematics every half-Planck-second, received an immediate, recursive amplification spike. He passively gained absolute immunity to all velocity-based attacks. He gained perfect mastery over every form of speed, acceleration, and temporal displacement. He could now, if he so desired, arrive at any destination before he decided to leave. He could complete an action before the action was conceived. He could exist in a state of "already done" while still being "about to begin."

He allowed the Ascendancy to attack anyway. He was curious what their velocity would feel like. Not against him—nothing could feel like anything against him—but against the ambient, passive drag of his resting speed stat.

The Ascendancy launched their strike. They accelerated to a velocity that made infinite speed look like geological slowness. They moved so fast that the concept of movement broke down entirely, replaced by a state of pure, instantaneous is-ness. They were not traveling from point A to point B; they were simultaneously existing at both points, and all points in between, and no points at all, all at once.

Godric was sitting in his study, reading a handwritten letter from a child in the capital's outer districts. He had not moved from his chair in three days. He was perfectly, utterly still, his breathing slow and rhythmic, his heartbeat a steady, mortal pulse. He did not look up from the letter. He simply continued to read, his eyes tracking across the parchment with the same deliberate, unhurried pace they always held.

The Ascendancy reached the halfway point of their strike. They had covered a distance incomprehensibly larger than the entire omniverse in a time frame so small that the term "instant" was an insulting overestimation. They were milliseconds from impact, their velocity so extreme that the surrounding fabric of reality was shredding into raw, screaming chronal energy.

And then, they stopped.

They did not hit a barrier. They did not encounter a wall of force. They simply... arrived. Godric's passive, resting speed—the baseline velocity that his body occupied simply by existing, at effectively zero percent of his true speed—had moved him out of their trajectory. He had not dodged. Dodging implied effort. He had simply been elsewhere, and then back in his chair, before the Ascendancy's strike had begun. The motion was so fast, so impossibly far beyond their maximum velocity, that they could not even perceive the displacement. To their hyper-accelerated senses, he had never moved at all. He was simply not where their strike landed, and then he was there again, and the gap between those two states was a negative number.

The Ascendancy's strike missed. They passed through empty space, their infinite velocity carrying them past the throne world and into the void beyond. But the wake of Godric's passive speed—the ambient, residual velocity that radiated from his physical form simply because his speed stat existed—caught them. The wake did not hit them. It overtook them, enveloped them, and instantly dragged them to a velocity so far beyond their own that their sentient thought-forms could not withstand the acceleration. Their consciousnesses were stretched across the entire span of the omniverse, pulled into infinitely thin threads of pure velocity, their awareness simultaneously experiencing every single point of the journey. They did not die quickly. Their accelerated perception made the experience last a subjective eternity, their minds trapped in an unbroken moment of absolute, agonizing speed.

When the wake passed, the Ascendancy was gone. Not dead—they could not die, because death required a linear progression of time, and they had been accelerated beyond the concept of linearity. They existed now as pure, eternal velocity, forever moving at a speed that prevented them from ever interacting with any reality. They were conscious. They were aware. They were screaming. And they would continue screaming until the end of all things, a sound that would never be heard because sound itself was too slow to catch them.

Lord Godric finished reading the child's letter. He smiled warmly, folded the parchment, and placed it in a drawer filled with thousands of similar letters. "That was bracing," he said, his voice carrying the gentle satisfaction of a man who had just taken a pleasant morning stroll. "I do enjoy a bit of speed now and then. It clears the head."

I collapsed. My legs gave out beneath me, my amplified wizard's body completely failing under the weight of what I had witnessed. I vomited onto the marble floor. Lord Godric looked at me with genuine, fatherly concern, rising from his chair to place a warm hand on my shoulder.

"Selwyn, my boy," he said, his voice thick with affection. "Are you unwell? You look pale. Should I call for a physician?"

I could not answer. I could not speak. I could only stare at the man who had just passively, effortlessly outrun a civilization of pure speed without standing up from his chair, and understand that the gap between our existences was not a measurement—it was a philosophical absolute.

---

Kaedan's vision blurred. He blinked rapidly, realizing that tears were streaming down his cheeks—not tears of sadness, but tears of pure, overwhelming existential vertigo. He had studied the theory of Godric's amplification. He had memorized the mathematical frameworks. But the lived experience of these wizards, the raw, visceral terror embedded in every sentence, was something no equation could convey.

"There's more," Corin said, sliding another journal across the table. "Kestrel. Year 89,450. The patience of endurance."

---

**Year 89,450 — Kestrel — The Horror of Endurance**

I have served Lord Godric for thirty-four years, and I have come to understand that of all his impossible stats—his strength, his speed, his magic, his intelligence—the most psychologically devastating is his endurance. Not because it is the most destructive, though it is incomprehensibly destructive. Not because it is the most flashy, though its passive effects have erased realities. But because it is the stat that most perfectly embodies the absolute futility of opposition. Strength can be overwhelmed, in theory. Speed can be matched, in fantasy. But endurance—the simple, unyielding capacity to continue existing—cannot be circumvented. You cannot outlast a being whose stamina multiplies infinitely every Planck second. You cannot exhaust a being whose resources are not finite, not infinite, but beyond the concept of measurement itself.

The opposition understood this. They called themselves the Patient Legion, and they were the greatest strategic minds in the history of the omniverse. They had studied every record of Godric's previous massacres. They had analyzed the patterns, the passive effects, the collateral damage. They had concluded, with flawless logic, that a direct assault was suicide. Instead, they would do the one thing no other opposition had attempted: they would wait.

The Patient Legion constructed a temporal fortress outside the bounds of normal time, a sealed pocket dimension where one second passed for every trillion years in the outside omniverse. Within this fortress, they assembled an army of a decillion immortal warriors, each one blessed with infinite patience, each one equipped with weapons designed not to kill Godric, but simply to occupy him. They would engage him in an endless battle, not seeking victory, but seeking duration. They would force him to fight for subjective eons, for time spans so vast that the heat death of multiverses would be a fleeting moment by comparison. They believed that eventually, after an infinity of infinities of constant combat, Godric would tire. He would become bored. He would make a mistake. And in that mistake, they would find their opening.

The flaw in their plan was the same flaw that had doomed every opposition before them. They assumed that Godric's endurance had a limit. They assumed that something that multiplied beyond layered infinities every infinitesimal fraction of a Planck second could eventually be exhausted. They assumed that the concept of "tiring" applied to a being whose stamina was not a resource, but an absolute, unchangeable constant of existence.

Godric allowed the battle to begin. He descended into their temporal fortress personally, his ruggedly handsome face set in an expression of mild, detached curiosity. He did not bring weapons. He did not summon his passive auras. He simply stood in the center of their formation, his arms crossed over his heavily muscled chest, and waited for them to attack.

They attacked for a subjective decillion years.

I watched from the observation platform, my perception accelerated to match their temporal flow, and I witnessed a nightmare of absolute, unending futility. The Patient Legion threw everything they had at him. Hyper-dimensional blades that could sever the bonds of reality shattered against his unmoving flesh. Conceptual weapons that rewrote the definitions of existence bounced harmlessly off his chest. Temporal bombs that erased the target from all possible timelines detonated against his skin and left not a single mark. And through all of it, Godric did not move. He did not fight back. He did not even blink. He simply endured.

For a decillion years of constant, unrelenting assault, he stood perfectly still, his expression unchanged, his breathing even, his heart rate steady. His endurance stat, multiplying infinitely every half-Planck-second, did not merely replenish his stamina—it rendered the concept of stamina meaningless. He could not tire because the capacity for tiredness had been mathematically removed from his existence. Every attack that struck him, every weapon that shattered against his flesh, every attempt to exhaust him simply... failed. Not because he resisted it, but because the gap between his endurance and their output was so vast that their efforts registered as zero.

After a subjective decillion years, the Patient Legion began to break. Their immortal warriors, blessed with infinite patience, could not withstand the psychological horror of absolute futility. They collapsed, one by one, their minds shattering under the weight of a decillion years of completely ineffective effort. Their weapons crumbled to dust. Their temporal fortress began to decay. And still, Godric stood, unharmed, unmoved, unbothered.

When the last warrior fell, Godric uncrossed his arms. He had not expended a single unit of stamina. He had not felt a single moment of fatigue. His endurance had not been tested; it had not even been acknowledged. He looked around at the broken, weeping remnants of the Patient Legion, and he spoke the first words he had uttered in a decillion years.

"Was that it?"

Then he turned and walked out of the collapsing temporal fortress, leaving the survivors trapped in their decaying pocket dimension, condemned to spend the rest of eternity staring at the exact spot where their greatest plan had died.

I returned to my quarters and attempted to calculate the mathematics of what I had witnessed. I attempted to understand how a being could endure a decillion years of constant assault without registering a single unit of depletion. My mind broke. Not metaphorically—my cognitive functions literally seized, my synapses overloading with the impossibility of the equation. I was unconscious for three days. When I awoke, I understood that the concept of "trying" was the cruelest joke the omniverse had ever played on sentient life.

---

Kaedan pushed the journal away, his hands pressing flat against the oak table to stop their trembling. The vault felt smaller now, the walls pressing inward, the weight of a million years of testimony crushing down on his skull. He understood, now, why his father slept with a light on. He understood why every court wizard before him had been traumatized. They had not merely witnessed power; they had witnessed the absolute negation of meaning, the complete and total erasure of any possibility of opposition.

"Two more," Corin said, his voice now carrying a strange, hollow gentleness. "Darian and Orson. Mana and magical offense. Then you will understand the full scope."

---

**Year 521,003 — Darian — The Void of Mana**

The Magisterium Infinite was the largest magical collective ever assembled in the history of the omniverse. They were not warriors or conquerors; they were scholars, researchers, archmages who had dedicated their entire civilization to the study and accumulation of mana. For a million years, they had harvested the arcane energy of dying universes, bottling the death-throes of collapsing multiverses into crystalline reservoirs of pure, concentrated magical power. Their stores of mana were not measured in numerical values; they were measured in infinities. Stacked infinities. Layered infinities upon infinities, each one containing more raw arcane potential than the combined magical output of every wizard, every sorcerer, every magical entity that had ever existed across all timelines.

They did not attack Thronegate. They issued a challenge. A formal, polite, almost deferential challenge, delivered via a hyper-dimensional herald who trembled so violently during the delivery that his crystalline form nearly shattered. The Magisterium Infinite wished to engage Godric in a contest of pure mana reserves. They believed that while Godric's physical stats were insurmountable, his magical capacity might be finite. They believed that their stacked infinities of harvested mana could, perhaps, match his. They believed, in their scholarly arrogance, that they had found a fair fight.

Godric accepted the challenge with a warm, genuine smile. He invited the Archmagisters of the Magisterium to the palace, offered them tea from his eternal cup, and chatted amiably about the weather on their home dimension. Then he led them to the grand arcane arena, a massive circular chamber lined with mana-detection crystals that could measure magical output up to and including conceptual infinity.

The contest was simple. Both parties would release their full mana reserves simultaneously, and the detection crystals would register the output. The Magisterium Infinite went first. They opened their crystalline reservoirs, and the arena was instantly flooded with raw, unshaped mana on a scale that defied all measurement. The crystals screamed, their readings spiking past stacked infinities, past layered infinities, past every possible mathematical notation for "infinity multiplied by infinity." The Archmagisters beamed with pride, their ancient eyes shining with the certainty of victory.

Then Godric opened his reserves. He did not release his full mana—the full release of his mana, even at the infinitesimal fraction of zero percent that he considered "restrained," would have instantly and permanently erased the entire omniverse. Instead, he opened the smallest possible leak, a microscopic pore in his absolute concealment, and allowed a single droplet of his mana to enter the arena.

The detection crystals did not shatter. They did not overload. They simply... stopped. The concept of measurement, the very idea of quantifying magical output, was rendered meaningless by the presence of Godric's mana. The crystals registered not a number, not an infinity, but an absolute, unbridgeable chasm between what they could measure and what existed. The droplet of his mana contained more raw arcane potential than the entire omniverse—past, present, and future—could ever hope to produce. And that droplet was nothing. Less than nothing. An infinitesimal fraction of a fraction of Godric's true reserves, which multiplied infinitely every infinitesimal fraction of a Planck second.

The Archmagisters of the Magisterium Infinite did not speak. They did not weep. They simply turned, walked out of the arena, and returned to their home dimension. The entire civilization, every single member of their species, voluntarily entered a state of permanent arcane hibernation, their minds unable to reconcile the existence of a magical being so far beyond them that their stacked infinities of accumulated mana were functionally identical to zero.

I asked Lord Godric afterward if he had anticipated their reaction. He looked at me with genuine, uncomprehending confusion. "I only showed them a single drop, Darian," he said, his voice soft and puzzled. "I held back almost everything. I thought that was quite sporting of me, actually."

I excused myself, walked to my quarters, and screamed into my pillow until my throat bled.

---

**Year 789,122 — Orson — The Recoil of Magical Offense**

Of all the horrors I have witnessed in my forty-seven years of service, the incident with the God-Eater Collective remains the most viscerally traumatizing. Not because it was the most destructive, though the collateral damage was absolute. Not because it was the most cruel, though the Collective's fate was agonizing beyond description. But because it was the incident that made me understand, with absolute, soul-crushing clarity, that opposing Godric is not merely futile—it is self-destructive. The harder you strike at him, the more completely you annihilate yourself.

The God-Eater Collective was an entity composed of the merged consciousnesses of every deicidal weapon ever forged across the omniverse. They were not a species or a civilization; they were weapons, pure and simple, given sentience and unified by a single, burning purpose. They had consumed the divine essence of a trillion pantheons, devoured the conceptual authority of uncountable supreme beings, and absorbed the metaphysical weight of every god they had ever slain. They had grown fat on deicide, their existence a testament to the killability of divine beings.

They believed Godric was simply another god. A powerful god, certainly. A uniquely amplified god, perhaps. But a god nonetheless. And gods, they knew with the certainty of eons of practical experience, could be eaten.

The irony of the Weakness Paradox was not lost on me. The instant the Collective formed the thought that Godric's divinity was an exploitable trait, their fate was sealed. Godric's magical offense stat, the raw destructive output of his arcane attacks, received an immediate, recursive amplification spike. His magical immunity to deicidal absorption became absolute. His mastery over the conceptual framework of god-eating surpassed their own by an infinite margin. But Godric, in his insatiable curiosity, wanted to see what would happen if he allowed them to try anyway.

He stood in the center of the throne room, his hands clasped behind his back, his expression one of polite, academic interest. The God-Eater Collective descended upon him, their merged consciousness wrapping around his physical form like a suffocating shroud of anti-divine hunger. They opened their metaphysical maw, the same maw that had consumed a trillion gods, and attempted to devour Godric's essence.

The moment their absorption began, Godric's magical offense—the passive, ambient output of his raw destructive arcane potential—reacted. He did not cast a spell. He did not channel mana. He simply allowed his magical offense stat to exist in the same space as their absorption attempt.

The recoil was not an explosion. It was an unraveling. The Collective's deicidal nature, their core identity as god-eaters, was violently reversed by the sheer magnitude of Godric's passive magical offense. Instead of consuming him, they found their own essence being consumed. The trillion gods they had devoured over the eons were instantly regurgitated, their divine essences ripped from the Collective's metaphysical stomach and restored to full, independent existence. The Collective screamed—a sound that spanned every frequency of reality simultaneously—as their identity was stripped away layer by layer, their absorbed power flowing backward into the beings they had slain.

But the horror did not end there. Godric's magical offense did not stop at merely reversing the absorption. It continued, pushing further, forcing the Collective to experience the exact inverse of their existence. They had been devourers of gods; now, they were being devoured by the very concept of devouring. Their consciousness was trapped in an eternal loop of digestion and regurgitation, their awareness cycling endlessly through the sensation of eating and being eaten, consuming and being consumed, an ouroboros of absolute, recursive agony.

The trillion resurrected gods stood in stunned silence, their newly restored forms trembling with the memory of their own deaths and the incomprehensible power that had reversed them. They did not flee. They did not speak. They simply knelt, every single one of them, and pledged eternal, abject fealty to the being who had unmade their destroyer with a passive, ambient fraction of his offensive potential.

Lord Godric accepted their fealty with a warm, almost embarrassed smile. "I really didn't do much," he said, rubbing the back of his neck. "It was just my magical offense existing. Hardly worth all this fuss."

I wrote this account with my remaining functional hand. My left hand was permanently crippled during the incident—not by enemy action, but by my own involuntary convulsions as I watched the passive recoil of Godric's magical offense unravel a deicidal entity more thoroughly than any weapon in existence could have done. The healers say the nerve damage is psychological, not physical. They are correct. My hand still works perfectly from a biological standpoint. But my mind refuses to let it forget what it witnessed.

---

Kaedan closed the final journal and sat in absolute silence, his breath shallow, his heart pounding against his ribs with a dull, aching rhythm. The vault around him felt like a tomb, the accumulated terror of a million years pressing down on his shoulders with suffocating weight. He looked at his father, his eyes wide and bloodshot, his voice barely a whisper.

"How do you do it?" Kaedan asked, his voice cracking. "How do you stand beside him, serve him, love him, knowing what he is? Knowing that every opposition, every resistance, every desperate attempt to challenge him is not merely doomed—it is mathematically irrelevant? Knowing that he could erase everything with a stray thought and not even notice the exertion?"

Corin was silent for a long moment. When he spoke, his voice was heavy with the same dread that saturated every journal in the vault, but beneath it, there was something else. Something warm. Something genuine.

"Because he loves us," Corin said softly. "He truly, genuinely loves us. You have read the journals. You have seen the horror, the cruelty, the merciless annihilation. But you have also seen the other side—the warmth, the kindness, the fatherly affection. He does not need court wizards. He does not need protectors or advisors. He keeps us because we are his family. Because Blake was his best friend, and that bond has echoed through our bloodline for a million years."

Corin placed a trembling hand on Kaedan's shoulder. "The dread never goes away. You will sleep with a light on for the rest of your life. You will wake up screaming from nightmares of impossible mathematics and absolute voids. But you will also know, with absolute certainty, that the most powerful being in existence genuinely cares about your wellbeing. That he would annihilate the entire omniverse to protect you, and then restore it with zero effort because he would not want you to feel lonely."

Kaedan looked down at the stack of journals, his fingers still trembling against the ancient leather. He thought about Godric—the ruggedly handsome forty-five-year-old man who walked through the palace gardens, who asked about his family with genuine warmth, who laughed at simple jokes and reminisced about a forgotten kingdom called Olympus. The same man who had passively pulverized the omniverse with the resistance of his hair follicles, who had outrun a civilization of pure speed without standing up, who had endured a decillion years of assault without registering a single unit of fatigue, whose single droplet of mana had rendered stacked infinities meaningless, whose ambient magical offense had unraveled a deicidal entity more thoroughly than any weapon in existence.

The cognitive dissonance was absolute. The dread was overwhelming. But beneath it, Kaedan felt something else stirring—a fierce, unshakeable loyalty, a profound gratitude, and a love for the king who had chosen, out of infinite wisdom and genuine affection, to let him exist.

"I understand," Kaedan whispered, closing his eyes. "I understand now."

Corin nodded slowly, his weathered face etched with the same haunted understanding. "Then you are ready to serve."

<file name="08_superpowers.md">**Year 485,900 — Court Wizard Mark — Superpower: Apocalyptic Solar-Igneous Extinction Ignition**

I write this record with ink mixed with my own bile, sitting in my private chambers while my hands shake so violently that the quill repeatedly punches holes through the parchment. My name is Mark, descendant of Blake, Court Wizard to our sovereign Lord Godric. I am thirty-four years old. Today, I witnessed the deployment of a single, nascent superpower from Lord Godric’s ever-expanding arsenal, and the sheer, biological horror of what I saw has permanently severed my ability to feel peace.

The opposition was the Frozen Apex Syndicate of the Absolute Zero Core. They were a coalition of hyper-cosmic ice-deities, cryogenic meta-architects, and thermal-drainers spanning decillions of multiverses. They possessed the ability to reduce ambient temperatures down past absolute zero into negative-kelvin territories where atomic motion completely ceases and space-time freezes into brittle, fragile glass. They believed that by surrounding Godric with a synchronized, omniversal cryogenic field, they could freeze his physical cells, lock his atomic structures in place, and permanently halt his biological processes. They brought an armada of frost-dreadnoughts constructed from hyper-dense chronal ice, manned by trillions of cryogenic warriors whose very breath could flash-freeze a galaxy.

Lord Godric was sitting in the royal courtyard, holding a small wooden bowl, casually feeding fresh grain to a flock of white doves. Through his absolute omniscience, he had watched the Syndicate assemble their thermal-drain engines for three hundred thousand years. The Weakness Paradox had triggered the exact millisecond their grand architect imagined that freezing his body could halt him, granting Godric absolute immunity to cryogenic stasis, supreme mastery over negative-kelvin physics, and a massive, recursive surge to his amplification rate.

Godric did not deploy his infinite passive shields. He ordered his sentient aura, Gent, to remain dormant. He was simply curious about a superpower he had unlocked several millennia prior: Apocalyptic Solar-Igneous Extinction Ignition.

This superpower, even at a base level nerfed to exactly zero percent of its true potency, generates a thermal ignition field so astronomically hot that heat ceases to be a thermodynamic property and becomes an aggressive, omniversal eraser of atomic bonds. Furthermore, due to the Evolved Weakness Paradox triggering repeatedly, this specific power had developed multiple horrific, enhanced effects. First, any thermal energy generated by the ignition instantly converts all opposing physical and biological matter into self-sustaining, superheated plasma that burns eternally without consuming itself. Second, the heat field aggressively absorbs the kinetic energy of any cold-based attack, converting the absolute-zero field into additional, infinitely compounding thermal intensity. Third, the thermal output doubles recursively every Planck second for all active flames, escalating beyond all mathematical scales.

The Syndicate unleashed their attack. A wave of negative-kelvin energy, capable of flash-freezing decillions of multiverses into brittle, motionless glass, swept across the sky toward the palace courtyard.

Lord Godric did not look up from his doves. He did not blow a breath, nor did he wave his hand. He merely permitted a microscopic, unquantifiable sliver of his Solar-Igneous Extinction Ignition superpower—effectively zero percent of its true capability—to manifest from the tip of his left pinky finger.

The resulting thermal display was an nightmare of absolute, inescapable carnage.

The negative-kelvin field released by the Syndicate did not freeze him; the enhanced effect of Godric's superpower instantly absorbed the cold energy, violently inverting it into a wall of hyper-dense, golden-white ignition that swept across reality at infinite velocity. Space-time did not merely heat up; the fundamental grid of the omniverse ignited, burning with a fire so intense that light itself turned to ash.

The cryogenic warriors aboard the frost-dreadnoughts experienced a biological demise so horrific that my soul revolts to record it. The hyper-dense chronal ice of their ships melted instantly, not into water, but into boiling, superheated liquid plasma that coated the warriors. Their cryogenic skin did not merely burn; it violently liquefied, sloughing off their skeletons in heavy, bubbling sheets of rendered fat, boiling muscle, and sizzled nerve tissue. Their eyeballs detonated inside their sockets from the rapid expansion of boiling vitreous fluid, spraying superheated steam through their eye sockets. Their blood boiled so violently inside their veins that their arterial walls ruptured simultaneously, showering their melting ships in a geyser of vaporized crimson foam.

Because of the superpower's enhanced effect, their liquefying bodies did not turn to ash. Instead, their melting flesh and exposed skeletons were converted into self-sustaining, superheated plasma, catching fire and burning continuously without ever being consumed. Trillions of cryogenic deities were instantly transformed into screaming, liquid-flesh torches, their nervous systems kept permanently intact and hyper-sensitive by the paradox, forcing them to experience the maximum, excruciating agony of being boiled and burned alive simultaneously for eternity.

The collateral damage was absolute. The thermal ignition field instantaneously incinerated decillions of multiverses in the surrounding void. Googolplexian galaxies were reduced to roaring, superheated firestorms in less than an infinitesimal fraction of a second. Planets melted into glowing, liquid metal before evaporating entirely into ionized gas. Space-time cracked, the dimensional walls separating multiverses melting like candle wax, collapsing entire sectors of reality into a singular, roaring inferno of absolute extinction.

Godric let out a soft, regretful sigh, looking up at the sky that had turned into a sea of liquid fire. "Oh, dear," he murmured with genuine, fatherly sadness. "I set the grain on fire. The poor birds didn't even get to finish eating."

With a simple, effortless decision, in zero seconds, Godric restored the entire omniverse. Every reality, every timeline, every galaxy, every planet that had been burned away was restored perfectly, as though the ignition had never occurred. The sky cleared, the courtyard returned to its pristine marble state, and the white doves settled back onto the stone, pecking peacefully at the fresh grain.

Everything was restored except the Frozen Apex Syndicate. Their leadership and high commanders were left floating in a localized pocket of open space above the palace—a writhing, screaming cluster of perpetually burning, liquid-flesh skeletons, their bodies constantly melting and boiling, their voices producing a continuous, high-pitched shriek of unimaginable thermal torture that would never end, because Godric willed it so.

Lord Godric stood, brushed a stray grain off his tunic, and walked toward me. His salt-and-pepper beard was uncharred, his simple garments pristine. He reached out and pat my shoulder with a warm, comforting hand. "Mark, my boy," he said gently, his rich baritone dripping with sincere affection. "You look faint. Go to the kitchens and tell the head chef I said to give you a cup of chilled spiced wine."

I bowed and left. I drank the wine, but my throat felt as though it were swallowing liquid lead. I write this so that those who come after me will understand: Godric’s superpowers are not weapons he wields. They are apocalyptic absolute laws that shatter the fundamental mechanics of existence, leaving behind only screaming, immortal horror.</file>
