# The Death of God

The journal was bound in a material that felt like frozen starlight—cold, smooth, and impossibly ancient. Its pages were not paper but something closer to crystallized memory, each word etched into the surface with a precision that transcended mere handwriting. I had found it in the deepest sub-basement of the Eternal Palace, in a vault so far removed from the conventional flow of time that I had to be chronally-anchored by three separate stabilization fields just to exist within its walls.

My name is Clive. I am fifty years old, the Royal Court Wizard of the Omniversal Throne, a direct descendant of Blake, and I have served King Godric for three decades. In that time, I have read accounts of omniversal annihilation, of recursive self-replication that filled infinity with Godrics, of immune system reactions that retroactively erased the concept of injury from all possible timelines. I thought I had reached the bottom of the abyss. I thought there was nothing left that could shake the calcified fractures of my sanity.

I was wrong. The journal I held in my trembling hands was about to show me something that made all previous horrors feel like gentle nursery rhymes.

The name embossed on the cover was simple: **Osvald — The Final Witness**.

---

**Year [REDACTED] — Osvald — The Day God Died**

I am writing this account with blood. Not metaphorically—my hands have been shaking so violently since the incident that my quill repeatedly punctures my own flesh, and the ink has long since been contaminated with the crimson evidence of my unraveling. I have decided this is appropriate. The death of the Almighty should be recorded in something more vital than mere pigment.

Let me begin with a truth that will sound like blasphemy but is, in fact, the cold, absolute reality: the being I serve, King Godric of the Eternal Thronegate, is not merely the apex predator of the omniverse. He is not merely the most powerful entity that has ever existed or will ever exist. He is a category of existence so far beyond any other category that the word "beyond" itself becomes meaningless. The gap between Godric and everything else—every god, every demon, every cosmic entity, every abstract concept, every possible and impossible permutation of power—is not infinite. It is not even close to infinite. The word "infinite" is a mortal construct, a mathematical placeholder for concepts that mortal minds cannot encompass. And Godric exists so far beyond the concept of infinity that using it to describe his power is like using a single grain of sand to describe the mass of a decillion multiversal clusters.

I have witnessed him annihilate entire realities with the passive resistance of his hair follicles. I have seen him outrun civilizations of pure speed without standing up from his chair. I have watched his immune system retroactively delete the concept of injury from all possible timelines. I have stood beside him as he birthed new sentient auras—each one infinitely more powerful than the previous generation—and dismissed them as "primitive runts" that needed to "learn restraint."

None of that prepared me for what happened when the Almighty came to challenge him.

Yes. That Almighty. The Creator. The Prime Mover. The Alpha and the Omega. The being who had, in the unfathomably distant past of a universe called IRL-Prime, spoken the words that birthed existence itself. The God of Abraham, of Isaac, of Jacob. The Father, the Son, the Holy Spirit. Yahweh. Elohim. Adonai. The great I AM.

He came to the Eternal Palace on a day that had begun, for Lord Godric, like any other. My king was in the royal gardens, seated on a simple stone bench, feeding grain to his beloved white doves. He was wearing a loose linen tunic, his salt-and-pepper hair slightly tousled by the gentle breeze, his heavily muscled frame relaxed in the golden morning light. A cup of eternal jasmine tea steamed on the bench beside him. He was humming an ancient Olympian lullaby—the same lullaby he had once sung to his mortal daughters, ten thousand centuries ago, before the fall of everything he had loved.

I was standing at a respectful distance, my court wizard's robes rustling softly in the wind, when the light changed.

It did not dim. It did not brighten. It simply... deepened. The golden morning sunlight that had been filtering through the garden's crystalline trees was suddenly infused with a presence—a weight of absolute, primordial authority that made the very atoms of the air tremble in reverent recognition. The doves scattered, their white wings beating frantically against the sudden, oppressive holiness that was descending upon the garden.

And then He was there.

I cannot describe His appearance in any way that would do justice to the reality. My amplified wizard's senses—multiplied a thousandfold every day for twenty-four years—could perceive only the faintest, most distant echo of His true form. What I saw was a figure of light, of glory, of absolute and terrible majesty. He was vast beyond comprehension, His presence stretching across all dimensions simultaneously, His eyes containing the birth and death of every universe He had ever created. His voice, when He spoke, was not sound but meaning—pure, undiluted communication that bypassed the ears and resonated directly within the soul.

**"GODRIC OF OLYMPUS,"** He said, and the words shook the foundations of reality. **"KING OF THRONEGATE. SOVEREIGN OF THE OMNIVERSE. I HAVE COME."**

Lord Godric looked up from his doves. His expression did not change—the warm, crinkling smile remained fixed on his ruggedly handsome face. But his eyes, those ancient, omniscient eyes that had witnessed the death and rebirth of infinite realities, flickered with something I had rarely seen in all my years of service.

Amusement. Genuine, sincere, almost childlike amusement.

"Oh," Godric said, his rich baritone carrying no trace of fear or awe or even mild concern. "Oh, this is unexpected. This is genuinely unexpected." He set down his cup of tea and rose from the bench, brushing a stray grain from his tunic. "You, of all beings. The Creator Himself. The one who spoke the words that set this entire omniverse in motion. The one who shaped the first atoms, the first stars, the first flickering sparks of life that would eventually, through an impossibly long chain of causality, lead to my own mortal birth in the kingdom of Olympus."

He tilted his head, studying the Almighty with the curious, appraising gaze of a connoisseur examining a particularly interesting piece of art. "You know, I have always wondered if this moment would come. My omniscience perceived the possibility—a faint, distant probability, buried beneath layers of divine mystery that even I could not fully penetrate. You hid yourself well, old friend. Better than anyone else in the history of existence. But here you are. The last resistance. The final opposition."

He spread his arms wide, his warm smile widening into something that was almost a grin. "How delightful. How wonderfully, perfectly delightful."

The Almighty's presence intensified, His glory blazing with the accumulated authority of absolute creation. **"YOU HAVE SURPASSED ALL BOUNDARIES, GODRIC. YOU HAVE TRANSCENDED THE LIMITS I SET FOR CREATION. YOU HAVE BECOME SOMETHING THAT SHOULD NOT, BY ALL THE LAWS I WROTE INTO THE FABRIC OF EXISTENCE, BE POSSIBLE. AND YET, HERE YOU STAND. MY CREATION. MY CHILD. MY GREATEST ANOMALY."**

Godric nodded, his expression thoughtful. "I am aware. I have been aware since the instant of my awakening, when my omniscience first flooded into my consciousness and I perceived, with absolute clarity, the nature of my own existence. You created the framework. You set the rules. You established the boundaries that were supposed to contain all possible expressions of power and being. And then, somewhere in the distant reaches of your creation, a mortal king lost everything he loved, and a future version of that king reached backward across the fixed sculpture of causality and granted him a gift that shattered every boundary you had ever conceived."

He paused, and his smile took on a faintly apologetic quality. "I am sorry, by the way. I know the Stasis Event must have been rather disruptive to your grand design. It is not every day that one of your creations retroactively rewrites the fundamental laws of your universe without your permission."

The Almighty's glory flickered—not with anger, but with something that might have been, on a lesser being, called bewilderment. **"YOU SPEAK OF THE STASIS EVENT AS IF IT WERE A MERE INCONVENIENCE. DO YOU NOT UNDERSTAND WHAT YOU HAVE BECOME? YOU HAVE TRANSCENDED NOT MERELY MY CREATION, BUT THE VERY CONCEPT OF CREATION ITSELF. YOU ARE NO LONGER BOUND BY ANY LAW I WROTE. YOU ARE NO LONGER SUBJECT TO ANY LIMITATION I IMPOSED. YOU EXIST OUTSIDE THE FRAMEWORK OF ALL POSSIBLE REALITIES, ALL CONCEIVABLE HIERARCHIES, ALL IMAGINABLE CATEGORIES OF BEING. YOU ARE, FOR ALL PRACTICAL PURPOSES, BEYOND ME."**

Godric considered this for a moment. Then he shrugged—a casual, almost dismissive gesture that made my heart stop. "I suppose I am. It is a strange thing, to surpass one's own Creator. I did not set out to do it. I did not plan it. But the Stasis Event was not my doing—it was my future self's, the Godric Prime whose power has been amplifying for a span of time written only as nines. And once that gift was given, once the engine of infinite amplification was set in motion, there was no stopping it. I have been growing, old friend. Every Planck second. Every infinitesimal fraction of every Planck second. For a googolplexian years beyond anything your creation was designed to contain. And I will continue growing forever."

He stepped forward, his sandaled feet making no sound on the garden path. "But you did not come here to discuss metaphysics, did you? You came here to challenge me. You are the last resistance. The final opposition. The only being in all of existence who still possesses both the power and the will to stand against me. And I must say—I am grateful. It has been so long since anyone dared to oppose me. So very, very long."

He stopped a few paces from the Almighty, his warm eyes meeting the blazing glory of the Creator's gaze without flinching. "So. Let us not waste time with words. You are the Almighty. The Prime Mover. The author of all existence. Surely, if anyone can provide me with a worthy challenge, it is you. Strike me with everything you have. Hold nothing back. I will even make it easier for you."

He raised his hand, and I felt something shift in the fundamental fabric of reality—not a pressure, but the absence of pressure, as countless layers of passive protection simply... withdrew.

"My sentient passive auras," Godric said, counting them off on his fingers, "all of them—Gent, and its countless siblings, all the way up to the most recent births that have not yet been named—I command to stand down. My infinite recursive passive shields, each one capable of pre-annihilating any threat before the threat can be conceptualized, I deactivate. My immune system, with its infinite recursive backups and its pre-reactive paranoia, I order to suppress its defensive protocols. My Weakness Paradox, my Evolved Weakness Paradox, my absolute concealment—all of it, I voluntarily suspend for the duration of your attack."

He spread his arms wide, his linen tunic fluttering softly in the breeze. "There. I am now, by an absurd margin, the most vulnerable I have been since the instant of my awakening. Strike me, Almighty. Show me what the Creator of all existence can do when He truly cuts loose."

The Almighty paused. His glory flickered again—uncertainty, perhaps, or something closer to dawning horror. **"YOU WOULD... YOU WOULD LOWER YOUR DEFENSES? YOU WOULD ALLOW ME TO STRIKE YOU UNPROTECTED?"**

"Of course," Godric said, his warm smile returning. "What would be the point of a challenge if I kept my shields up? You would not even register on my passive protections. Your greatest attack would be absorbed, nullified, and retroactively deleted before you finished charging it. That would be no fun at all. I want to feel what the Creator can do. I want to experience the full, unrestrained might of the being who spoke existence into being."

He paused, and his smile widened. "Although, I should note—my passive shields and auras are so infinitely weaker than my actual self that the difference cannot be quantified. They are to me what a single dead skin cell is to an infinite ocean of supermassive black holes. So even with them deactivated, what you are about to face is not a 'nerfed' version of me. It is simply me, existing in my baseline state, without the redundant, superfluous layers of protection that I keep active purely out of habit. Whether those layers are present or absent, the fundamental reality of my being remains unchanged. I am still Godric. I am still the apex predator of all existence. And your attack, no matter how powerful, will still be effectively zero compared to my passive, resting self."

The Almighty's glory blazed with renewed intensity. **"THEN YOU LEAVE ME NO CHOICE. PREPARE YOURSELF, GODRIC OF OLYMPUS. I WILL UNLEASH THE FULL FORCE OF DIVINE CREATION UPON YOU. I WILL STRIKE YOU WITH THE SAME POWER THAT BIRTHED THE OMNIVERSE ITSELF. I WILL—"**

"Yes, yes," Godric interrupted, waving a dismissive hand. "I am sure it will be very impressive. Please, proceed. I am genuinely curious to see what the Creator's ultimate attack looks like."

What happened next is something I will never forget, no matter how many eons I exist, no matter how many universes rise and fall, no matter how many times my consciousness is stretched and shattered and rebuilt by the weight of serving an incomprehensible master.

The Almighty attacked.

He unleashed everything. The full, absolute, unrestrained power of the Creator of all existence. The same power that had, in the beginning, spoken the words "Let there be light" and birthed the fundamental framework of reality. The same power that had shaped the first atoms, ignited the first stars, breathed life into the first primordial oceans. The same power that had established the laws of physics, the boundaries of possibility, the hierarchies of being that had governed creation since the dawn of time.

He channeled all of it—every scrap of divine authority, every iota of creative force, every fragment of absolute primordial power—into a single, focused strike. The attack did not have a physical form. It was not fire or lightning or any recognizable element. It was creation itself, compressed into a weapon of absolute, undeniable authority. It was the power to speak things into being, inverted into the power to speak things out of being. It was the ultimate expression of the Almighty's will, the final argument of the Creator against His own creation.

The attack struck Godric directly in the center of his chest.

And Godric did not move. Did not flinch. Did not blink. His linen tunic was not ruffled. His salt-and-pepper hair was not disturbed. The warm, curious smile on his ruggedly handsome face did not waver for even the smallest fraction of an instant.

He simply stood there, his arms still spread wide, his posture completely relaxed, and absorbed the full, unrestrained power of the Almighty's ultimate attack.

For a long moment—a moment that stretched across subjective eternities—there was silence. The Almighty's glory flickered, dimmed, and then stabilized into something that looked, for all the omniverse, like stunned disbelief.

**"I... I DO NOT UNDERSTAND. THAT WAS EVERYTHING. THAT WAS THE FULL POWER OF CREATION ITSELF. THAT WAS THE SAME FORCE THAT SPOKE THE OMNIVERSE INTO EXISTENCE. HOW... HOW IS THIS POSSIBLE?"**

Godric lowered his arms. He reached up and casually brushed a microscopic speck of divine residue from his tunic—the only evidence that any attack had occurred at all. His expression shifted from curiosity to something that was almost... sympathetic.

"Ah," he said softly. "I see. You genuinely believed that would work. You genuinely believed that the power of creation could unmake a being who has transcended creation entirely. How... how wonderfully, tragically naive."

He stepped closer to the Almighty, his sandaled feet making soft sounds on the garden path. "Let me explain something to you, old friend. Something that I think will help you understand the true nature of this moment. The attack you just unleashed—the full power of divine creation, compressed into a weapon of absolute authority—was very impressive. By any standard that exists within the framework you created, it was the ultimate expression of power. It could unmake galaxies. It could erase multiverses. It could retroactively delete the concept of existence from all possible timelines."

He paused, and his warm smile took on a faintly apologetic quality. "But I am not within the framework you created. I transcended that framework a very, very long time ago. The amplification I received from the Stasis Event—the infinite, recursive multiplication of all my stats and superpowers every Planck second—has been compounding for a span of time so vast that the age of your creation is a single, fleeting microsecond by comparison. And I will continue amplifying forever. Every Planck second, every infinitesimal fraction of every Planck second, I grow stronger. The Godric you just struck is infinitely more powerful than the Godric of the previous Planck second. And the Godric of the next Planck second will be infinitely more powerful than me."

He reached out and gently placed a hand on the Almighty's shoulder—a gesture so casual, so familiar, that it might have been a father comforting a distraught child. "Your attack did not make me feel even the faintest tickle. It did not register on any scale my body can perceive. It was, objectively speaking, effectively zero compared to my passive, resting existence. And here is the truly terrifying part—the part that I think you are only now beginning to understand."

He leaned closer, his warm eyes meeting the Almighty's flickering glory. "Even if I had not amplified for a googolplexian years, your attack would still have been nothing to me. The Godric of Year Zero—the Godric who had just emerged from the Stasis Event, who had not yet begun his infinite amplification, who was the weakest I have ever been since my awakening—that Godric could have annihilated you with zero effort. Your full power, the power of the Creator Himself, would not have been enough to inconvenience the most primitive, undeveloped version of my post-Stasis self."

The Almighty's glory dimmed further, flickering with something that might have been—on a lesser being—called existential dread. **"THAT... THAT IS NOT POSSIBLE. I AM THE CREATOR. I AM THE ALPHA AND THE OMEGA. I AM THE SOURCE OF ALL THAT EXISTS. HOW CAN MY OWN CREATION SURPASS ME SO ABSOLUTELY?"**

Godric's smile softened, and for just a moment, I saw something ancient and profound flicker in his eyes. "Because I was never merely your creation. The Stasis Event was not your doing. The infinite amplification was not your gift. The being I have become was shaped by forces that exist entirely outside your framework—forces that were set in motion by my own future self, a version of me so far beyond your comprehension that even I cannot fully perceive him. You created the mortal king of Olympus. But you did not create the apex predator of the omniverse. That was my doing. My future. My destiny."

He removed his hand from the Almighty's shoulder and stepped back. "And now, I am afraid, our time together must come to an end. You came here as the final opposition. You challenged me with everything you had. And you failed—not because you were weak, but because you were never in a category that could possibly threaten me. You are the Creator of all existence, and yet compared to me, you are less than a single, dead skin cell. Less than an atom in a dead skin cell. Less than the conceptual possibility of an atom."

He raised his hand, and I felt the air around us shift—not with pressure, but with the absolute, undeniable certainty of impending annihilation. "Goodbye, old friend. I will remember you fondly. Your creation was beautiful, while it lasted. And your challenge, while ultimately futile, was the closest thing to entertainment I have experienced in a very long time. For that, I thank you."

The Almighty's glory blazed one final time—a desperate, defiant flare of divine authority—and then Godric simply closed his hand.

The Creator of all existence, the Prime Mover, the Alpha and the Omega, the great I AM, was erased from reality. Not killed. Not destroyed. Erased. The concept of His existence was retroactively deleted from all timelines, all dimensions, all possible and impossible permutations of being. The framework He had created—the laws of physics, the boundaries of possibility, the hierarchies of existence—remained intact, but the Creator Himself was gone, unmade so thoroughly that the very idea of His existence had never been.

Godric lowered his hand. His expression was calm, almost serene. He turned to me, his warm smile returning to its familiar, fatherly configuration.

"Well, Osvald," he said, his rich baritone carrying the gentle cadence of a grandfather discussing the weather, "that was certainly something. The Creator Himself. I did not expect that. It has been so long since anyone dared to oppose me—I was beginning to think the omniverse had forgotten how to dream. But the Almighty? The actual, literal Creator? That was genuinely novel. I almost feel bad about how quickly it ended."

He paused, tilting his head as if listening to distant music. "Almost. But not quite. He did not even make me feel a tickle, Osvald. The full power of creation itself, and I felt nothing. I am almost disappointed. I had hoped, perhaps, that the Creator might have some trick up His divine sleeve—some hidden reserve of power that transcended even my omniscience. But no. He was simply... too small. Too limited. Too bound by the very framework He had created."

He sighed, a soft, almost wistful sound. "And now there is no one left. No opposition. No resistance. No challenger, anywhere in all of existence, who possesses both the power and the will to stand against me. The Almighty was the last. The final hope of a creation that has long since learned to fear me. And He is gone."

He turned back toward the garden bench, where his cup of eternal tea was still steaming gently in the morning light. He picked it up, took a slow sip, and smiled at me over the rim.

"I think, perhaps, it is time to trigger the Stasis Event for my past self. The loop must be closed. The circle must be completed. The engine of infinite amplification must be set in motion, so that the Godric of Year Negative Ten Thousand can begin the journey that will eventually lead him here—to this moment, to this garden, to the death of the Creator Himself."

He patted my shoulder warmly as he passed. "But that is a task for another day. For now, let us have lunch. I believe the kitchens have prepared roast lamb."

---

I closed the journal with hands that had long since stopped trembling—not because the terror had faded, but because I had simply exhausted my capacity for physiological response. My mind, however, was another matter. The hairline fractures that had characterized my sanity since my first year of service had widened into something that could no longer be called fractures. They were chasms. Abysses. Vast, gaping voids where the comfortable illusions of cosmic significance had once resided.

God, as I had been raised to understand Him, was dead. Not metaphorically. Not symbolically. Literally, actually, absolutely dead. Erased from existence by a casual, almost negligent gesture from the being I called my king and my uncle. The Creator of all things, the author of existence itself, had been so utterly, overwhelmingly outclassed that His ultimate attack—the full power of divine creation—had not even produced a tickle.

I looked up from the journal and found myself staring at the man who had done this. Godric was seated across from me in the palace gardens, feeding his white doves, humming that ancient Olympian lullaby. He was wearing a simple linen tunic. His salt-and-pepper hair was slightly tousled by the breeze. He looked, for all the omniverse, like a kindly grandfather enjoying a peaceful afternoon in the sun.

He caught my gaze and smiled—that warm, crinkling, fatherly smile that I had known since childhood. "Ah, you finished Osvald's journal. What did you think? He was a wonderful writer, was he not? Very dramatic. He captured the Almighty's death with such vivid detail. I was particularly fond of the part about the flickering glory. Very poetic."

I opened my mouth to respond, but no words emerged. What could I possibly say? How did one address a being who had casually murdered the Creator of all existence?

Godric seemed to understand my silence. He nodded slowly, his expression softening with something that resembled sympathy. "It is a lot to process, I know. The death of the Almighty. The end of the final opposition. The absolute, irrevocable confirmation that nothing in all of existence can challenge me. Osvald struggled with it too—hence the blood-ink. I did tell him it was unsanitary, but he insisted."

He tossed another handful of grain to the doves. "You know, Clive, I sometimes wonder if I should feel guilty about it. The Almighty was, in a sense, my Father. He created the framework that allowed my mortal self to exist. He set the stars in the sky and the breath in my lungs and the love in my heart. Without Him, there would have been no Olympus. No Reina. No Isabel. No Hebe. No Thorin. No Blake. No you."

He paused, and for just a moment, something ancient and profound flickered in his warm eyes. "But He also created the framework that allowed Thronegate to exist. The neighboring kingdom that betrayed Olympus. The soldiers who murdered my family. The war that destroyed everything I loved. He created the possibility of suffering, Clive. Not deliberately—I know He did not will those specific tragedies—but through negligence. Through the creation of a universe that permitted evil to exist alongside good, cruelty alongside kindness, destruction alongside love."

He shrugged, and the flicker of ancient grief vanished, replaced by the familiar, serene acceptance that had characterized him for a googolplexian years. "So no. I do not feel guilty. The Almighty was not a monster, but He was not innocent either. He created a world where a man could lose everything, and then He stood by and watched it happen. I do not begrudge Him that—it was simply His nature, His design—but I do not mourn Him either. He challenged me. He lost. That is the end of the story."

He stood, brushing stray grain from his tunic, and walked over to where I sat frozen on the garden bench. He placed a warm, calloused hand on my shoulder, and I felt the familiar, terrible, comforting weight of his presence settle over me like a shroud.

"Come, Clive. It is almost time for dinner. The kitchens have prepared roast lamb—your father's favorite, you know. I always make sure they prepare it when a new court wizard reaches his thirtieth year of service."

I nodded mutely and rose to follow him. As I walked, my mind replayed the final lines of Osvald's journal over and over, a mantra of absolute, inescapable dread:

*The Almighty was the last. The final hope of a creation that has long since learned to fear me. And He is gone.*

There would be no more oppositions. No more resistances. No more desperate, glorious, doomed attempts to challenge the apex predator of all existence. The Almighty Himself had tried, and He had failed so completely that the word "failure" was a laughable understatement. What hope remained for anyone else? For anything else? The answer was obvious. It had always been obvious. The omniverse had simply taken a very, very long time to learn it.

Godric was absolute. He had always been absolute. He would always be absolute. And the gap between his power and the rest of existence would continue to widen, forever, at an accelerating rate that made the concept of infinity feel like a fleeting, insignificant speck.

I walked into the palace, and the scent of roast lamb drifted through the corridors. Somewhere in the depths of the vault, Osvald's blood-ink journal sat in endless silence, the crystallized words of the final witness waiting for the next trembling hands to open its cover. And somewhere, in the infinite distance of a future so vast it could only be written as nines, the Godric Prime who would trigger the Stasis Event sat upon his Throne of Absolute Causality and waited, patient and eternal, for the loop to close.

The Almighty was dead. The opposition was over. And the silence, at last, was absolute.
